newsitem.title: USA: Farrakhan supporters gather outside U.N.
newsitem.headline: Farrakhan supporters gather outside U.N.

text.p: Fiery Black Moslem leader Louis Farrakhan and thousands of his supporters gathered in New York on Wednesday to commemorate the first anniversary of the Million Man March on Washington by black men.

The rally on streets outside the United Nations -- billed as the "World's Day of Atonement" -- began with early morning prayers. Speeches were scheduled later in the day by Farrakhan, South African politician Winnie Mandela and comedian and activist Dick Gregory.

"I pray that the people of New York will turn out and you will see an outpouring again of our people because we believe that only when you can reconcile with God and get clear with him that he will empower us to unify and change the realities under which we live," Farrakhan said before the rally.
By mid-morning more than a thousand people had taken their places in the Dag Hammarskjold Plaza across from the U.N. headquarters. About 20 blocks of midtown Manhattan were closed to traffic.

Unlike last year's huge march in Washington, this event included women and children. Organisers said it was an attempt to bring together men, women and children for a day of prayer, speech and personal affirmation. There would also be appeals to countries around the world to end abuses of power and wealth.
"I was in D.C. last year and I'm trying to continue with the movement," said participant Bob Burnett, who came from Kansas City, Missouri, to join the march.
"Last year they brought all the men together and they went back to spread the word to the sisters," he said. "It's time for them to come."
Many of the women wore long flowing white robes, while many men wore the dark suits and red bow ties that are distinctive of Farrakhan's followers in the Nation of Islam, a U.S. Black Moslem group.
The speeches by Farrakhan and others were to be broadcast by satellite to 50 countries around the world, according to organisers.

Farrakhan, who has been accused of anti-Semitism, said he also hoped to meet with some Jewish leaders in New York. Since last year's march, designed as a day of self-reliance and affirmation, he has made controversial visits to Libya, Cuba, Iraq, Iran, Nigeria and Sudan.
One of the march organisers said that Wednesday's event would have a positive message.

"This is not an anti-Semitic demonstration, an anti-white demonstration. Atonement is for everybody," said Benjamin Chavis, a Christian minister and the former head of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.

Jewish groups had hoped to hold counter-demonstrations, and New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani said he refused to take part in the day's event because of what he called Farrakhan's "rhetoric of hatred."

The mayor promised marchers, however, that police "will make certain that they are not harmed in any way, that they're not harassed and that they have the opportunity to make the point they want to make."
